Question: Equiangular hexagon \(ABCDEF\) has side lengths \[AB=CD=EF=1\] and \[BC=DE=FA=r.\] The area of \(\triangle ACE\) is \(70\%\) of the area of the hexagon. What is the sum of all possible values of \(r?\)
Solution:
The alternating side lengths suggest completing the hexagon to an equilateral triangle. An equiangular hexagon has interior angles
\[
\frac{(6-2)180^\circ}{6}=120^\circ.
\]
Extend the sides \(BC\), \(DE\), and \(FA\) until their lines meet. At each added corner, the angles next to the hexagon are \(60^\circ\), so each added corner triangle is equilateral. Its side along \(AB\), \(CD\), or \(EF\) has length \(1\), so all its sides have length \(1\). Each side of the outer triangle therefore consists of lengths \(1,r,1\), making the outer triangle equilateral with side \(r+2\).

For an equilateral triangle of side \(s\), the altitude is
\[
\sqrt{s^2-(s/2)^2}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}s.
\]
Its area is consequently \(cs^2\), where \(c=\sqrt3/4>0\). Subtracting the three added unit triangles gives the hexagon's area \(H\):
\[
H=c(r+2)^2-3c
=c(r^2+4r+1).
\]
Now join \(A,C,E\). The portion of the hexagon outside \(\triangle ACE\) consists exactly of \(\triangle ABC\), \(\triangle CDE\), and \(\triangle EFA\). Each has adjacent sides \(1\) and \(r\) with included angle \(120^\circ\). Its height over the unit side is \(\sqrt3 r/2\), obtained from the same equilateral-triangle altitude calculation, so each area is \(cr\).

These three triangles account for \(30\%\) of \(H\). Thus
\[
3cr=\frac3{10}c(r^2+4r+1).
\]
Canceling the positive factor \(3c\) yields
\[
r^2-6r+1=0,
\qquad (r-3)^2=8.
\]
Hence \(r=3\pm2\sqrt2\). Both values are positive. For either value, cutting equilateral corners of side \(1\) from an equilateral triangle of side \(r+2>2\) constructs the required hexagon, so both solutions are admissible. Their sum is
\[
(3+2\sqrt2)+(3-2\sqrt2)=\boxed6,
\]
choice \(\text{E}\).
